course.learn: This section focuses on **People** within **Capacity planning**. Capacity planning ensures people, technology, and infrastructure can handle expected workload, security tooling, growth, and failure conditions. Security controls themselves consume compute, storage, bandwidth, and staff time.
course.why: Insufficient capacity can become an availability problem or force teams to disable security controls under load.
course.example: A SIEM deployment estimates log volume and retention storage before onboarding thousands of new endpoints.
course.exam: Consider staffing, training, automation, compute, storage, network capacity, redundancy, and growth—not just server CPU.

course.learn: This section focuses on **Infrastructure** within **Capacity planning**. Infrastructure monitoring observes networks, cloud configuration, appliances, links, and supporting resources. NSM analyzes network behavior, while CSPM evaluates cloud security posture and misconfiguration.
course.why: Infrastructure telemetry helps detect both attacks and unsafe configuration drift.
course.example: CSPM flags a public storage bucket while NSM detects unusual outbound traffic from a server subnet.
course.exam: NSM = network activity. CSPM = cloud configuration/posture.

breakdown.explanation: Use duplicate components or paths so one failure does not stop the service.
